sections.h2: Who records deeds in Wood County, Ohio?
sections.html:
The Wood County Recorder records deeds, mortgages, plats and releases for every parcel in the county. The office sits on the second floor of the County Office Building at One Courthouse Square in Bowling Green, and the main number is 419-354-9140. Counter hours run Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Bowling Green has been the county seat since 1870, when the county seat moved from Perrysburg. The county covers 620 square miles along the Maumee River and belongs to the Toledo metropolitan area. The 2020 census counted 132,248 residents, and the county's own housing stock of 56,863 units is about two thirds owner occupied. That mix of university town, river suburbs and farm parcels means the Recorder handles everything from a Perrysburg subdivision lot to a township acreage split.

Ohio splits the work among three county offices. The elected Recorder keeps the official records, the Auditor transfers taxable ownership, and the Treasurer bills and collects the tax. A seller needs all three offices in the right order.

sections.h2: What does a deed need before Wood County will record it?
sections.html:
It needs the grantor's signature, a notary or other authorized acknowledgment, and a legal description that matches the chain of title. Ohio Revised Code 5301.01 requires the grantor to sign and then acknowledge the signing before a judge or court clerk, a county auditor, a county engineer, a notary public or a mayor.

Ohio Revised Code 5301.25 sends the deed to the Recorder of the county where the land lies. Until a deed is recorded, the statute calls it fraudulent against a later buyer who paid in good faith and had no notice of it. When a survey was made of the land being conveyed, the Auditor requires the surveyor's name to appear in the deed.

The Recorder's site also publishes document standards and a fee calculator. A few habits keep a deed from bouncing back:

  • Cite the prior deed by instrument number or by volume and page.
  • Reference the original instrument whenever you record a release, affidavit or correction.
  • Use the exact legal description from the last recorded deed unless a survey changed it.
  • Bring the Auditor's endorsement, since the Auditor handles the deed before it reaches the Recorder.

sections.h2: How much does the Wood County Recorder charge to record a deed?
sections.html:
The base charge in Ohio Revised Code 317.32 is a $17 recording fee plus a $17 housing trust fund fee for the first two pages. Each later page adds $4 plus $4. A county may also add a document preservation surcharge of up to $5, and the Recorder's online calculator on the county site shows the estimate for your document.

The statute prices pages at eight and one half by fourteen inches, so a long legal description or an oversized exhibit can add pages. The table lists the items a house seller meets most often.

Recording items under Ohio Revised Code 317.32 that apply to a Wood County house sale
ItemAmount in the statute
First two pages of an instrument$17 base fee plus $17 housing trust fund fee
Each additional page$4 base fee plus $4 housing trust fund fee
Document preservation surchargeUp to $5, set by the county
Marginal reference in a separate instrument$2 base fee plus $2 housing trust fund fee per reference
Photocopy after recording$1 plus $1 per page in the statute; the Wood County Recorder lists $2.00 per page

Source: Ohio Revised Code 317.32 and the Wood County Recorder contact page.

sections.h2: What happens at the Auditor's office before the deed is recorded?
sections.html:
The deed goes to the Wood County Auditor first. Under Ohio Revised Code 319.202 the buyer files a statement declaring the value of the property, and the Auditor endorses the deed with the conveyance fee amount before the Recorder accepts it. The Auditor's office phone is 419-354-9150, and the Auditor is on the second floor of the same County Office Building.

Ohio Revised Code 319.54 sets the conveyance fee at one dollar, or ten cents for each one hundred dollars or fraction of one hundred dollars of value, whichever is greater. The grantor pays it. Some transfers pay nothing, including gifts between spouses or between parent and child, transfers among heirs of one decedent for no money, and transfers into a trust the grantor can revoke.

Separately, Ohio Revised Code 322.02 lets a county commissioners' board levy a real property transfer tax of up to thirty cents per hundred dollars of value. When a county levies it, the grantor pays the Auditor before the deed goes to the Recorder. Ask the Wood County Auditor whether any county transfer tax is in force before you set a closing budget.

sections.h2: How do I look up or copy a recorded document in Wood County?
sections.html:
Start with the online search on the Recorder's site. The Adaptable Visual Access index covers records from 1980 and runs about one day behind the filing date. Document images come through a Laredo Anywhere account, which the office describes as meant for high volume professional use and which requires an account request form. Older book indexes are available through the AmeriScan Documents-On-Demand service.

Ohio Revised Code 317.13 requires every county recorder to post electronic indexes and images of instruments recorded on or after January 1, 1980, and to offer electronic recording of conveyances. The statute's deadline for both was June 30, 2026, and the statute bars a fee just to create a login or view the indexes.

For paper copies, the Wood County Recorder charges $2.00 per page. Requests must include an instrument number or a book and page reference, and staff do not open documents to hunt for legal descriptions. If you need that reference, search the index first:

  • Search by grantor or grantee name in the index.
  • Write down the instrument number shown beside the match.
  • Send the number with the page count you want to the Recorder by phone or email.

sections.h2: What if the Recorder refuses a document or a mortgage release is missing?
sections.html:
The Recorder may refuse an instrument that the Revised Code does not authorize for recording or that looks materially false or fraudulent. Ohio Revised Code 317.13 then lets the person who presented it ask the Common Pleas Court to order recording, and the court will do so if the instrument is authorized and not fraudulent.

A more common problem for sellers is a mortgage that was paid years ago but never released of record. Ask the lender for a release, and have it recorded with a marginal reference to the original mortgage so the index links the two. Call the Treasurer at 419-354-9130 about taxes still due on the parcel.

faqs.q: How much is the recording fee for a Wood County deed?
faqs.a: The statute sets $17 plus $17 for the first two pages and $4 plus $4 for each later page, and the county may add a preservation surcharge of up to $5. Use the fee calculator on the Wood County Recorder's site for a figure on your document.

faqs.q: Does Wood County charge a transfer tax on a sale?
faqs.a: Ohio charges a conveyance fee through the Auditor on most sales, paid by the grantor. A county transfer tax exists only if the commissioners levied one under Revised Code 322.02, so ask the Wood County Auditor at 419-354-9150.

faqs.q: Can I get a copy of my deed without going to Bowling Green?
faqs.a: Yes. Search the online index for the instrument number, then send the request by phone or email with that number. The Recorder lists copies at $2.00 per page.

faqs.q: How far back do the online Wood County records go?
faqs.a: The index covers 1980 forward and trails the filing date by about a day. Earlier records sit in book indexes that the Recorder makes available through its imaging partner.

faqs.q: Who is responsible if the deed is signed but never recorded?
faqs.a: Recording is the grantee's protection. Under Revised Code 5301.25 an unrecorded deed can lose to a later good faith buyer, so record the deed right after closing.
